analysis.one_liner: Bans requiring workers to pay union dues or fees as a condition of employment nationwide.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by 30 Republican senators, the bill received no hearing or vote and died in committee when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal labor law to ban 'union security' agreements, the contracts that let a union and an employer agree that workers covered by a union contract must join the union or pay fees for the representation they receive. About half the states already ban this under state 'right-to-work' laws; this bill would impose that rule on the whole country, including rail and airline workers. The bill was introduced in February 2015, sent to the Senate labor committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who prefer not to join or financially support a union would keep their full job without paying dues or fees. Employers would also gain: unions covered by this rule must represent every worker in the bargaining unit while collecting dues only from volunteers, which leaves unions with fewer resources and gives employers more leverage at the bargaining table.

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the sections of the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act that allow union security agreements requiring employees to join a union or pay fees as a condition of employment [S2].
Also ends the provision allowing railroad carriers to require payroll deduction of union dues or fees under such agreements [S2].
Its stated purpose is to protect the choice of individual employees to join or refrain from joining a labor organization [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Labor unions would bear the main cost: they would remain legally required to represent all workers in a bargaining unit but could collect dues only from members who choose to pay, reducing their funds and membership. Workers who rely on union bargaining would face weaker representation as union resources shrink.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unions and the workers they represent

drawbacks.text: Under the bill, unions would still be obligated to represent every worker in a bargaining unit but could no longer require nonmembers to pay fees for that representation, a dynamic commonly called the 'free rider' problem, which shrinks union resources [S2].

Stricter versions of this rule have already been adopted at the state level in roughly half the states; making it national would remove the choice of states and workers who prefer the current system [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a clear benefit to individual workers who object to paying union fees, but the cost lands on the institutions that negotiate wages and working conditions for millions of workers. Because unions would have to keep representing nonpayers while collecting dues from fewer people, their capacity to bargain would shrink, and most labor economists expect wages and union strength to fall as a result. The gain to individual objectors is real but narrow; the loss to collective worker power is broad.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the bill in the Senate on February 5, 2015, joined by 14 original cosponsors including Majority Leader Mitch McConnell [S5].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the record before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Unions and the workers who rely on them kept the existing system intact, since the bill never advanced; employers did not gain the bargaining leverage the bill would have provided.

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 14 original cosponsors including the Senate Majority Leader.

for.name: 29 of 54 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing or markup appears in the record for the entire two-year Congress.

against.name: Labor unions
against.what_they_did: Opposed national right-to-work legislation, which would bar unions from collecting required fees from the workers they represent.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a recorded vote.

industries.note: Unions would lose the ability to require fees from the workers they are legally required to represent, cutting their dues base and weakening their bargaining capacity. That capacity is what negotiates wages and conditions for the workers themselves.

With unions weaker and poorer, employers would face less resistance on wages and working conditions. The bill's benefit to individual non-union workers comes alongside this shift of leverage toward management.
